title: Which Came First: The Plan, or the Resources?

posts.author: TMS
posts.body: I have a question primarily aimed at people who have completed RPG Maker projects. Did you begin with a vision of the game that you wanted to make, and then went hunting for or created the resources needed to make it happen? Or did you begin by assessing the available resources and then build a game around what was most feasible? I know it probably wasn't that cut and dry, but I'm curious what method initially predominated.

posts.author: SGHarlekin
posts.body:
It's always the plan first. This "Asset shopping" is exactly why so many beginners never finish anything imho.
Know what you what you want to make, then look for the assets to make it happen. "Build a game around what is most feasible" doesn't really happen, because there are resources for pretty much everything, so all that ends up happening is people grabbing all this cool stuff and feature bloating their game, getting burned out, and never finishing anything.
Just like building a house, you don't go around just preparing random materials you thought looked cool. You make a plan of the things your house needs and then prepare exactly that.

I also bought a huge collection of music files, with over 1000 tracks. I used 2 songs in the jam so far...

I’ve been making sporadic attempts at game design using RPG Maker for a long time now, and what I currently plan to be my first completed game is one that relies entirely (or almost entirely) on the RTP graphics/music, not so much in hopes of making a masterpiece as just to prove to myself (and maybe others) that I can actually finish something. Of course, I wouldn’t be satisfied with making something completely generic, so I’m putting my own personality and interests into it, and am hoping to turn the self-imposed restrictions into a strength instead of a weakness. posts.author: Avery
posts.body:
For me it goes in tandem?
Like, if I have an idea, I'm gonna check out the style I'm planning to use and see what that offers. Some artstyles just make it incredibly hard to make certain types of games or map out certain areas. If we talk RTP, I usually roughly gather stuff that looks useful while doing this research, and after that, I can get a clearer idea of my vision with the knowledge what's available. If I would want to use paid packs, I would get a clear idea what they have, if I can combine them with another style, what that one has... Choosing a style might also go hand in hand with how easy I can edit/match it, so I would rather have something I can edit/expand myself without looking off.
Maybe I wanted a certain anthro race, but there are no resources, so I tweak the story to work with a different fantasy race that already has exisiting chars or I planned a certain area that I just cannot get the resources for without a lot of work or money so I see if I can get the same gameplay experience or story placed in another setting.
Never forget: your player doesn't know your original vision, so altering your concept is only between you and yourself and I personally would try to minimize the extra resource work from the concept stage on.
And when I get deeper into, I still might to smaller swaps, depending on what is out there and what I can reasonably do. Because: while I could technically in fact make any resource I might need, the time investment is not always worth the impact it would have on the overall result.
It is a whole different cup of tea if you do the art completly yourself. I made that for three finished projects, and bascially then I make a clear plan of the gameplay, and the minimum of resources needed, make those, and then if I have time and motivation left in the end make some more decorative clutter or something nicer. I also did not make the prettiest style I could, but made sure I could finish resources for a whole project in a reasonable time, opting for a simpler shading and limited palette.
In one case, where I had complex puzzles, I made placeholders, created the puzzles, tweaked the placeholders as needed and then made the real resources.
In all cases I work with placeholders until I am 100% sure the costum resource is worth the (time) investment. I would be pretty angry at myself making a custom SV battler for a char whichs design is not final and has to me made completly new afterwards again.

If you need the money to do so, just follow my sound (and patient) advice on it:
Save $5 every week for the end of dev cycle.  Make a list of every asset you need to replace.  When the game is "complete", go purchase the assets you need from a single artist (or artists who can meet the same aesthetic of assets, so you don't have clashing resources in your project) and begin replacing.  The replacing process doesn't take long at all, and if you ever finish your game, you should have a pretty chunk of cash to blow on assets.
I've been working on my game for 10+ years.  52x5= 260. 260*10= 2600.  It's a good chunk of cash to be sitting on when you need to go asset shopping.
You could also always acquire the talent to make some of your own resources.  Though, that will take effort and dedication to do so if you don't have the talent for it (or, you may be like me and hopelessly unable to do it, no matter what you learn, because your brain just isn't wired that way).
No matter what you do in life, the "Plan" is always the important part you should do first.  That plan allows you flexibility.  It reduces overhead (money spent, time spent, etcetera) on a project.  It keeps you from engaging in "feature bloat" (whether you're building a game, building a house, or deciding how to live your life).  Having that plan would also prepare you for fixing problems down the line.  Or... you could do what the Doom Bathroom guy did...  Basic idea, some things you want to do that "look cool" and no real plan for how it should come together until you've already removed all the supports for a giant bathtub on a second floor house, so that if you filled it with water, it'd slam into the first floor.
Yes, you should google "Doom Bathroom" to get the full story of what happens when you "try to plan around an idea and some assets", rather than creating the plan before any of the assets.

posts.author: JohnDoeGames
posts.body:
Tai_MT said:
The replacing process doesn't take long at all, (...)
Click to expand...
Well, that depends. Specially with sprite sheets. When you buy the assets (and they are not specially made for you) then your new tilesets will probably have all items on different positions and sizes. And your faces, and your character and... and... Everything that comes in a sheet.
With a little bad luck, you spend days, even weeks worth of editing.
When all the assets are custom made, then it they are probably named and formatted correctly, and all you have to do is overwrite your current assets (after you made a backup, don't forget the backup).
But the downsides to custom art are:
- They take time
- They are more expensive
If you have the money to spare or the talent to make them yourself, then there are also clear upsides:
- You have more freedom since your not limited to the assets present in a pre-made bundle
- Your art is unique, and I guess I don't need to explain why that's a huge selling point.

posts.author: Solar_Flare
posts.body:
I more or less agree with Tai_MT. While there are valid reasons to stick to the preset assets (aka "RTP"), if you have a specific vision in mind, it makes more sense to scrap most of the preset assets and commission assets specifically for your game.
I say "most of" because some of the preset assets are pretty basic and universal enough that it might not be worth scrapping them. This mainly refers to the tilesets, and
maybe
the icon set or battle backs. It all depends on what you want for your game though.
But it's true that this has the downside of being more time-consuming and expensive. If you're making a free game, and it's an original story (not, say, a fan game of something or other), and you want to stick to mostly preset assets, there's nothing wrong with that. You could say that that's why the preset assets exist.

I see your point, but it's mostly a "non-issue".  A lot of artists tend to leave your tilesets and such in the same basic "order" that the defaults are in for easy replacement (short of its some weird specialized set or something, which usually just means you redraw the map and not much else).
Cliffs tend to be left where cliffs are... grass and water... where they are... on and on.
Tilesets of objects would typically have to be made "custom" for you, so that they are actually on a tileset you can use with them.  Otherwise, you end up using a lot of just events for your object or whatever, since it doesn't exist on the tileset you need it to.  But, it's also not that difficult to move stuff around on a "tileset" yourself to get it to be an "easy replace" on your own, either.  Protip:  It's a lot of "copy+paste", and not a lot else to move assets around on the existing sheets.  At least, as long as what you're moving is "in the correctly formatted space" for it.
With a large game, you might spend about a month replacing assets...  With the average RPG Maker game (which doesn't even usually break 10 hours of playtime), it's maybe 3-7 days to replace all your assets.  And that's if you're only spending like 3 hours a day doing it.
When I replace, I tend to just shove the assets into the correct folders, then tell the game to call those assets, whatever they're named, instead of what I've already got.  The longest part is usually just setting "passability" again, or minor event reworks for animations and such.

posts.author: HB_Games
posts.body:
I believe you'll increase your chances of completing your game if you start with the assets you already have. In my case, I can create graphics, but I'm limited by the audio and plugins I can find or purchase, so I always keep that in mind before I begin.
Actually, even with graphics, I tend to impose limitations on myself—things like a specific number of expressions, character animation frames, battler animations, etc.
And I sincerely think this is a good thing. Constraints are great for creativity.

posts.author: TMS
posts.body:
It's interesting to see how opinions differ. Seems like most people (among those who have commented) are in the plan-first camp, and you all make some good arguments. I agree that cobbling a bunch of disparate resources together would be a mess. One would have to limit themselves to resources that have a certain amount of stylistic resemblance among them (though I guess it could be neat to do a game where each major area is in a different art style).
I'm not 100% sure if it would be a better idea to start a game using existing resources and then replace them later (if possible), or to make sure that all the resources a game idea requires can be obtained (even if it means commissioning them up front) before beginning to put the hard work in. I guess in the former case at least you'll have a game, even if you can't get it to look and feel the way you want it to, whereas in the latter case progress on the game might indefinitely stall for whatever reason and then you're out the time and/or money used to create those resources ahead of time.
@HB_Games
is right, of course, that constraints can lead to creativity. What I hope to be my first completed game is going to be made using RTP graphics/audio/code only, mostly because if I can't finish something a game that simple I may as well give up on my more ambitious projects. And I am trying to turn these self-imposed limitations into some sort of positive. The game's premise and plot, for example, take them into account and are somewhat informed by them. Still, I don't think that such restrictions are strictly necessary.

While I'd certainly _recommend_ this, I wouldn't say it's _absolutely necessary_ that all the resources share a stylistic resemblance. If you just want to focus on making a story, the art merely needs to be functional, not pretty. Of course, there are people who would be turned off your game by that, but maybe those are also the kinds of people who'd just skip through the story, so maybe your game is not for that kind of person.
TMS said:
I'm not 100% sure if it would be a better idea to start a game using existing resources and then replace them later (if possible), or to make sure that all the resources a game idea requires can be obtained (even if it means commissioning them up front) before beginning to put the hard work in.
Click to expand...
I don't think it's a good idea to make sure all the resources needed are commissioned before getting started, because then you've spent all that money and still have nothing to show for it. It's better to build your game with placeholder graphics and replace them later. In the case of an RPGMaker game, that could mean using the character generator to make placeholders (character generator graphics usually don't look too good, but they're definitely functional) or manually drawing bad terrain art by hand.
Starting with the art is _possible_ and has been done (a game I worked recently on started by hiring an artist and only later brought on programmers) but I would never recommend it. Though if it's a free game that doesn't require anything too exotic, it might be a more reasonable thing to do.
